newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy seeks return to European exchange rate mechanism.
newsitem.headline: Italy seeks return to European exchange rate mechanism.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Friday the lira's return to the European exchange rate mechanism was imminent after Rome lodged a formal request to be readmitted after a four-year absence.
Prodi told Italian news agencies while on a trip to Sicily that the lira would be back in the exchange rate mechanism in a matter of "a few hours or a few days."
The odds shortened on a swift lira return to the currency grid when Italy asked a key European Union monetary policy body to meet Saturday.
Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio confirmed from Frankfurt that the Italian government had asked to be let back into the currency grid.
European Union officials in Brussels said the EU monetary committee would meet Saturday to discuss the Italian request.

Prodi said that, while there were no formal talks between Italy and its partners, "we are exchanging the necessary data for a lira return to the ERM," according to the ANSA news agency. "That is the way it is going. These are not formal negotiations," Prodi said.

The monetary committee meeting, to be attended by central bankers and senior treasury officials from EU member countries, would be entrusted with agreeing on the central rate of exchange between the lira and the other currencies in the grid.
Italy has said it is determined to take the lira back into the exchange rate mechanism to establish its credentials as a prime contender to join European economic and monetary union in 1999.
A European Commission spokesman in Brussels said he could not confirm or deny that the Italian government had requested the meeting. There was no immediate comment from Rome.

Market speculation that Italy could make its move within hours was sparked Friday when Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in Frankfurt that the Italian government would "seek the re-entry of the lira into the ERM in November."
That suggested that Italy intended to bring the lira back into the currency grid either this weekend or next.
In Frankfurt, Ciampi appeared to signal that differences had receded between Italy and France and Germany over the appropriate parity level for the lira's return.

France, whose competitive edge was blunted when the lira lost about 30 percent of its value after its 1992 exit from the exchange rate mechanism in a currency crisis, is concerned that the lira should not be brought back at too high a rate.
With the lira's return looking likely this weekend, financial market speculation turned to the central "parity rate" that would be set between the lira and other currencies.
The lira was forced out of the ERM in September 1992 when a crisis of confidence in international financial markets over Italy's indebted finances precipitated a run on the currency.
